'''Kenneth J. Sterling''' (July 29, 1920 – January 12, 1995) was a medical doctor and prominent researcher on the topic of [[Thyroid hormones|thyroid hormone]] and [[human metabolism]]. He made significant discoveries on thyroid hormone activation and treated patients at the [[Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center]] for over thirty years.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/record/archives/vol20/vol20_iss16/record2016.27.html|title=Kenneth Sterling, Thyroid Expert, Dead at 74|date=February 10, 1995|work=Columbia University Record|issue=16|volume=20|access-date=Oct 2, 2016}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=http://www.cumc.columbia.edu/psjournal/archive/archives/jour_v15n2_0027.html|title=In Memoriam: Faculty|date=Spring 1995|work=P&S Journal|issue=2|volume=15|access-date=Oct 2, 2016|archive-date=March 30, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170330121627/http://www.cumc.columbia.edu/psjournal/archive/archives/jour_v15n2_0027.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Early life and friendship with H. P. Lovecraft==
Sterling was born in [[Baltimore, Maryland|Baltimore]], Maryland in 1920.

At the age of 14, Sterling became acquainted with  [[H.P. Lovecraft]] when his family moved to [[Providence, Rhode Island|Providence]] and he began attending Classical High School. He saw Lovecraft frequently during this time (1935–36), then corresponded with him when he went to Harvard in the fall of 1936. he collaborated with Lovecraft on "[[In the Walls of Eryx]]" (January 1936). Aside from the early memoir, "Lovecraft and Science" (in [[Marginalia (collection)|''Marginalia'']]), 1944, Sterling wrote the poignant reminiscent article "Caverns Measureless to Man" (''Science-Fantasy Correspondent'', 1975) about Lovecraft. This article quoted extensively from his letters to Lovecraft, which have not otherwise been widely available. It is hoped that his heirs will deposit these letters in an institution in the course of time.<ref>''The New Lovecraft Collector'' 10 (Spring 1995), p. 1</ref> Lovecraft's letters to Sterling as based on transcripts held by [[Arkham House]] have been published in the volume H. P:. Lovecraft, ''Letters to Robert Bloch and Others'', ed. David E. Schultz and S. T. Joshi. NY: Hippocampus Press, 2015.

When he was sixteen, Sterling enrolled in the undergraduate program at [[Harvard University]], from which he graduated in 1940. As an undergraduate student, he published his first scientific paper at the age of 19.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|date=1997-10-01|title=The Third International Workshop on Resistance to Thyroid Hormone|journal=Thyroid|volume=7|issue=5|pages=809–816|doi=10.1089/thy.1997.7.809|issn=1050-7256}}</ref>

Sterling then went to [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]], where he earned his medical degree in 1943 at the age of 23.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/01/27/obituaries/dr-kenneth-sterling-thyroid-specialist-74-dies.html|title=Dr. Kenneth Sterling, Thyroid Specialist, 74, Dies|last=Saxon|first=Wolfgang|date=1995-01-27|newspaper=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331|access-date=2016-10-02}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1958, Sterling joined [[Columbia University]] as a research associate at the [[Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons|College of Physicians & Surgeons]]. In 1962 he was appointed assistant clinical professor of medicine and became staff physician in [[nuclear medicine]] and director of the protein research laboratory at the [[James J. Peters VA Medical Center|Department of Veterans' Affairs Medical Center in the Bronx]], New York City. In 1970, Sterling became associate clinical professor of medicine, later rising to full [[clinical professor]] in 1974.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" />

== Research impact ==
[[File:Sterling and Yalow receiving Middleton Award 1973.png|thumb|264x264px|Kenneth Sterling, M.D. (center), receiving the Middleton Award with [[Rosalyn Sussman Yalow|Rosalyn Yalow]], Ph.D. (left) and Bronx VA Medical Center Director, Harold Jaffrey (right)]]
Sterling was one of the first researchers to use [[radioactive iodine]] to treat [[thyroid disease]]s.  He used [[Radioisotopic labelling|radioisotopic labels]] to study the metabolism of human [[serum proteins]] and [[red blood cell]]s.<ref name=":3" />  He discovered that the body converts the [[Prohormone|pro-hormone]] [[thyroxine]] into triiodothyronine, the primary active form of thyroid hormone.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2006-12-01|title=The endocrine society 2007 laureate awards|journal=Endocrine Reviews|volume=28|issue=5|pages=590–601|doi=10.1210/edrv.28.5.3451|issn=0163-769X|pmid=17722366|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>"[https://www.endocrine.org/~/media/endosociety/files/about-us/sawin/lewisbraverman_transcript.doc?la=en Lewis E. Braverman]." Interview by Michael Chappelle. ''Oral and Video History Interviews''. The Endocrine Society, 22 June 2014. Web. 2 October 2016.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/combinedannualre00colu_20|title=Combined annual report of the Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center|date=1960-01-01|publisher=Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center|via=Columbia University Libraries}}</ref> This breakthrough led to a new field of thyroid hormone research and led to the first early studies on the mechanism of action of thyroid hormones.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Sterling developed the equilibrium dialysis method for measuring free thyroxine, which remains the gold standard for evaluating free hormone levels in blood today.<ref name=":2" /> Sterling was a pioneering investigator identifying mitochondrial [[thyroid hormone receptor]]s, shortened [[Protein isoform|isoforms]] of the full-length, [[nuclear receptor]]s. He wrote a chapter on thyroid hormone receptors in the fifth edition of ''Werner's The Thyroid: A Fundamental and Clinical Text'', which is known as "the bible of modern thyroidology."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cooper DS|date=1987-07-03|title=Werner's the thyroid: A fundamental and clinical text|journal=JAMA|volume=258|issue=1|pages=111|doi=10.1001/jama.1987.03400010115045|issn=0098-7484|pmc=1494034}}</ref>

In 1972, Sterling was awarded the [[William Shainline Middleton|William S. Middleton]] Award for Excellence in Research, the highest honor of the VA Medical Center.<ref name=":0" /> He was cited for developing the <sup>51</sup>Cr labeling of red blood cells for clinical applications.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://permanent.access.gpo.gov/gpo37496/ORD-85yrHistory.pdf|title=A historical look at the establishment of the Department of Veterans Affairs Research & Development Program|last=Hays|first=Marguerite Hays|date=2010|website=U.S. Government Publishing Office|publisher=Department of Veterans Affairs Research & Development Program|access-date=2016-10-02}}</ref>

== Death ==
Sterling continued treating patients at the Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center up until a few days before he died. He died on January 12, 1995, while at his home in [[Riverdale, New York|Riverdale]], New York, at the age of 74. The probable cause of death was complications of an [[aneurysm]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> The International Workshop on Resistance to Thyroid Hormone, a biannual research forum, dedicated its third meeting to Sterling in 1997.<ref name=":2" />

*Sterling, K., Brenner, M.A. (1966) Free thyroxine in human serum: simplified measurement with the aid of magnesium precipitation. ''Journal of Clinical Investigation''.
*Sterling, K., Bellabarba, D., Newman, E.S., Brenner, M.A. (1969) Determination of triiodothyronine concentration in human serum. ''Journal of Clinical Investigation.''
*Sterling, K., Brenner, M.A., Newman, E.S. (1970) Conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine in normal human subjects. ''Science''.
*Braverman, L.E., Ingbar, S.H., (1970) Sterling, K. Conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3) in athyreotic human subjects. ''Journal of Clinical Investigation''.
*Sterling, K., Brenner, M.A., Saldanha, V.F. (1973) Conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine by cultured human cells. ''Science''.
*Sterling, K., Saldanha, V.F., Brenner, M.A., Milch, P.O. (1974) Cytosol-binding protein of thyroxine and triiodothyronine in human and rat kidney tissue. ''Nature''.
*Sterling, K., Milch, P.O., Brenner, M.A., Lazarus, J.H. (1977) Thyroid hormone action: the mitochondrial pathway. ''Science''.
*Sterling, K., Lazarus, J.H., Milch, P.O., Sakurada, T., Brenner, M.A. (1978) Mitochondrial thyroid hormone receptor: localization and physiological significance. ''Science''.
*Sterling, K., Brenner, M.A., Sakurada, T. (1980) Rapid effect of triiodothyronine on the mitochondrial pathway in rat liver in vivo. ''Science''.
